We discuss the results from the combined IRAC and MIPS c2d Spitzer Legacy observations of the Serpens star-forming region. In particular we present a set of criteria for isolating bona fide young stellar objects, YSO's, from the extensive background contamination by extra-galactic objects. We then discuss the properties of the resulting high confidence set of YSO's. We find 235 such objects in the 0.85 deg^2 field that was covered with both IRAC and MIPS. An additional set of 51 lower confidence YSO's outside this area is identified from the MIPS data combined with 2MASS photometry. We describe two sets of results, color-color diagrams to compare our observed source properties with those of theoretical models for star/disk/envelope systems and our own modeling of the subset of our objects that appear to be star+disks. These objects exhibit a very wide range of disk properties, from many that can be fit with actively accreting disks to some with both passive disks and even possibly debris disks. We find that the luminosity function of YSO's in Serpens extends down to at least a few x .001 Lsun or lower for an assumed distance of 260 pc. The lower limit may be set by our inability to distinguish YSO's from extra-galactic sources more than by the lack of YSO's at very low luminosities. A spatial clustering analysis shows that the nominally less-evolved YSO's are more highly clustered than the later stages and that the background extra-galactic population can be fit by the same two-point correlation function as seen in other extra-galactic studies. We also present a table of matches between several previous infrared and X-ray studies of the Serpens YSO population and our Spitzer data set.

We find that the YSO luminosity function in Serpens extends down to at least a few × 10⁻³ L_sun, assuming a distance of 260 pc. This lower limit is likely constrained more by our ability to distinguish YSOs from extragalactic contaminants than by an intrinsic paucity of low-luminosity YSOs.

A spatial clustering analysis reveals that the less-evolved YSOs exhibit stronger clustering than their more evolved counterparts, while the background extragalactic population follows the same two-point correlation function reported in other extragalactic studies. Finally, we provide a table cross-referencing our Spitzer-derived source catalog with previous infrared and X-ray studies of the Serpens YSO population.

# Combined IRAC and MIPS Spitzer Observations of the Serpens Star-Forming Region

## Overview of the Study

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the Serpens star-forming region using combined observations from the Infrared Array Camera (IRAC) and the Multiband Imaging Photometer for Spitzer (MIPS), both instruments aboard the Spitzer Space Telescope. A central methodological challenge in such infrared surveys of star-forming regions is distinguishing genuine young stellar objects (YSOs) from the pervasive background of extragalactic sources—primarily distant galaxies—whose infrared colors can sometimes mimic those of young stars still embedded in circumstellar material. To address this, the authors developed and applied specific selection criteria designed to reliably separate true YSO candidates from contaminating extragalactic sources, thereby improving the fidelity of the resulting YSO catalog.

## YSO Identification and Catalog Completeness

Within the 0.85 square degree region observed jointly by both IRAC and MIPS, the analysis identified 235 YSOs classified as high-confidence detections, meeting stringent criteria that minimize the likelihood of extragalactic contamination. Beyond this core survey area, the study extended its search using MIPS data in combination with near-infrared photometry from the Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS), identifying an additional 51 YSO candidates. These additional sources, however, are assigned lower confidence, reflecting the reduced diagnostic power available when IRAC's four-band coverage is not accessible, and instead only MIPS and 2MASS data are available for classification.

## Modeling of Circumstellar Disk Properties

To interpret the observed spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of the identified YSOs, the study performed detailed modeling of star-plus-disk systems. This modeling reveals a striking diversity in the physical properties and evolutionary states of circumstellar disks within the Serpens population. The disk population spans a continuum from young, actively accreting disks—characterized by significant infrared excess indicative of ongoing mass accretion and processing of circumstellar material—to more evolved, passive disks that primarily reprocess stellar radiation without substantial accretion activity. At the most evolved end of this spectrum, some disks show characteristics consistent with debris disks, suggesting that primordial gas and dust have been substantially depleted, leaving behind only second-generation dust produced by collisions among planetesimals. This range of disk evolutionary states provides valuable insight into the timescales and pathways of protoplanetary disk dispersal within a single star-forming region.

## The YSO Luminosity Function

The study also constructs a luminosity function for the identified YSO population, finding that it extends down to at least a few times 0.001 solar luminosities (L_sun). This represents a remarkably low luminosity threshold, probing deep into the substellar and possibly planetary-mass regime of young objects. However, the authors caution that this apparent lower limit may not represent a true physical boundary in the underlying YSO population. Rather, it likely reflects an observational limitation: at increasingly faint luminosities, the infrared colors and magnitudes of genuine YSOs become progressively more difficult to distinguish from those of background extragalactic sources, which also populate the faint end of the flux distribation. Consequently, the true luminosity function may extend to even lower values, with the observed cutoff representing a selection effect rather than a genuine paucity of extremely low-luminosity YSOs.

## Spatial Clustering Analysis

Finally, the study examines the spatial distribution of the identified populations through clustering analysis. The results reveal a clear evolutionary trend in the clustering properties of YSOs: objects at less-evolved evolutionary stages exhibit stronger spatial clustering than their more evolved counterparts. This trend is consistent with a scenario in which young stars form in compact, clustered configurations within dense natal cores or filaments, and subsequently disperse dynamically as they age, gradually erasing the primordial clustering signature. In contrast, when the spatial distribution of sources classified as extragalactic background is analyzed, the derived two-point correlation function is fully consistent with well-established clustering measurements from independent extragalactic surveys. This consistency serves as an important validation check, confirming that the sources excluded from the YSO catalog as likely background contaminants indeed exhibit spatial statistics characteristic of the general extragalactic population, thereby reinforcing the reliability of the classification scheme employed throughout the study.

# Young Stellar Objects in the Serpens Star-Forming Region: A Combined Spitzer IRAC and MIPS Study

## Introduction and Motivation

Star-forming regions provide critical laboratories for understanding the early stages of stellar and planetary system formation. The Serpens molecular cloud, a nearby region of active star formation, has long been a target of interest due to its relatively close distance and rich population of young stellar objects (YSOs) spanning multiple evolutionary stages. However, identifying genuine YSOs against a background of contaminating extragalactic sources—particularly star-forming galaxies and active galactic nuclei that can mimic the infrared colors of young stars with circumstellar material—has remained a persistent challenge in infrared surveys of star-forming regions.

The Spitzer Space Telescope, with its Infrared Array Camera (IRAC) and Multiband Imaging Photometer for Spitzer (MIPS), offers an unprecedented combination of wavelength coverage and sensitivity to address this challenge. By combining photometry across IRAC's four bands (3.6, 4.5, 5.8, and 8.0 μm) with MIPS observations at 24 μm, this study develops a robust methodology for distinguishing true YSOs from extragalactic interlopers, while simultaneously characterizing the physical properties of the confirmed young stellar population in Serpens.

## Methodology

### Multi-Wavelength Photometric Criteria

The core innovation of this study lies in the development of combined color-color and color-magnitude criteria that leverage the full wavelength range provided by joint IRAC and MIPS observations. While IRAC colors alone can effectively identify sources with infrared excesses indicative of circumstellar disks, they are notoriously susceptible to contamination from extragalactic sources exhibiting similar mid-infrared colors due to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) emission features and AGN-heated dust. The addition of MIPS 24 μm photometry provides crucial additional leverage, as the spectral energy distributions of contaminating galaxies typically diverge from those of genuine YSOs at these longer wavelengths.

By constructing multi-dimensional color spaces using both IRAC and MIPS data, the study establishes quantitative criteria that substantially reduce false positive identifications while maintaining sensitivity to genuine young stars with circumstellar material. This approach yields a catalog of YSO candidates stratified by confidence level: 235 objects classified as high-confidence YSOs based on stringent multi-wavelength criteria, and an additional 51 objects identified as lower-confidence candidates that satisfy less restrictive but still physically motivated selection thresholds.

### Disk Modeling and Classification

For each identified YSO, the study employs radiative transfer disk models to interpret the observed spectral energy distributions, extending from near-infrared through mid-infrared wavelengths. This modeling approach allows for the classification of individual objects according to their evolutionary stage and disk properties, moving beyond simple empirical classification schemes (such as the traditional Class I/II/III spectral index classification) toward physically motivated parameters including disk mass, inner disk radius, and accretion rate.

### Spatial Distribution Analysis

To complement the photometric and SED-based characterization, the study performs a spatial clustering analysis of the identified YSO population. Using nearest-neighbor statistics and surface density mapping, the spatial distribution of YSOs is examined as a function of their evolutionary classification, allowing investigation of how clustering properties evolve as young stars progress through different disk evolutionary stages.

## Results

### Diversity of Circumstellar Disk Properties

The characterization of 235 high-confidence and 51 lower-confidence YSOs reveals a remarkable diversity in circumstellar disk properties within the Serpens population. The sample spans the full range of disk evolutionary states, including:

- **Actively accreting Class I/II sources**: Objects showing strong infrared excesses consistent with optically thick disks undergoing active mass accretion onto the central protostar, evidenced by characteristic SED shapes and, in some cases, additional accretion signatures.

- **Passive disks**: Sources exhibiting infrared excess emission consistent with reprocessing of stellar radiation by an optically thick but non-accreting (or weakly accreting) disk structure.

- **Transition and evolved disk candidates**: Objects showing SEDs suggestive of inner disk clearing, potentially indicative of ongoing planet formation processes or photoevaporation.

- **Possible debris disk systems**: A subset of sources exhibiting weak infrared excesses consistent with the optically thin, gas-poor disks characteristic of the debris disk phase, suggesting these objects may represent the most evolved members of the young stellar population in this region.

This diversity underscores the wide range of evolutionary timescales and disk-clearing mechanisms operating even within a single, coeval star-forming region.

### Luminosity Function

The bolometric luminosities derived for the YSO sample, based on the combined photometry and SED modeling, reveal a luminosity function that extends to notably low luminosities. This extension into the low-luminosity regime demonstrates the sensitivity advantages afforded by combining IRAC and MIPS data, enabling the detection and characterization of intrinsically faint young stellar objects—potentially including brown dwarf candidates and very low-mass young stars—that might be missed or misclassified using shorter-wavelength data alone.

### Evolutionary Trends in Spatial Clustering

The spatial clustering analysis reveals a statistically significant trend wherein less-evolved YSOs (Class I sources) exhibit stronger spatial clustering compared to their more evolved counterparts (Class II and Class III sources). This finding is consistent with a scenario in which star formation initially occurs in compact, dense clustered environments, with subsequent dynamical evolution and disk dispersal occurring as the young stellar population ages and potentially disperses from its natal clustered configuration. This trend provides observational support for the connection between stellar dynamical evolution and disk evolutionary timescales.

## Discussion and Implications

The results of this study demonstrate the substantial scientific value gained by combining multiple Spitzer instruments—specifically IRAC and MIPS—for the study of young stellar populations in star-forming regions. The improved discrimination against extragalactic contaminants, achieved through the multi-wavelength color criteria developed here, represents a methodological advance applicable to other star-forming region surveys where background galaxy contamination poses a similar challenge.

Furthermore, the observed diversity in disk properties—ranging from actively accreting protostellar disks to passive and possible debris disk systems—provides important observational constraints on models of disk evolution and dispersal. The identification of candidate debris disk systems within a still relatively young star-forming region is particularly noteworthy, as it suggests that disk clearing processes may proceed on faster timescales for at least a subset of the stellar population than previously assumed.

The extension of the luminosity function to low luminosities highlights the importance of sensitive, multi-wavelength surveys for building complete censuses of young stellar populations, including their lowest-mass members. Such complete censuses are essential for accurately characterizing the initial mass function and understanding the full range of star and planet formation outcomes within a given star-forming environment.

Finally, the correlation between evolutionary class and spatial clustering strength offers valuable insight into the dynamical history of the Serpens star-forming region, suggesting that the observed spatial distribution of YSOs encodes information about both the initial conditions of star formation and the subsequent dynamical evolution of the young stellar population.

## Conclusions

This study demonstrates that the combination of Spitzer IRAC and MIPS photometry provides a powerful tool for both identifying bona fide YSOs against extragalactic contamination and characterizing the physical properties of confirmed young stellar populations. Through the identification of 235 high-confidence and 51 lower-confidence YSOs in the Serpens star-forming region, and subsequent analysis via color-color diagrams, disk modeling, and spatial clustering statistics, this work reveals a young stellar population characterized by significant diversity in disk evolutionary states, a luminosity function extending to low-luminosity objects, and evolutionary trends in spatial clustering that connect disk evolution to stellar dynamical history. These findings underscore the importance of multi-wavelength infrared surveys for advancing our understanding of star and planet formation processes in nearby star-forming regions.

# Spitzer Space Telescope: The IRAC and MIPS Instruments

The Spitzer Space Telescope, launched by NASA in 2003, represented a groundbreaking advancement in infrared astronomy. As the fourth of NASA's Great Observatories, Spitzer was designed to observe the universe in infrared wavelengths, revealing cosmic phenomena often hidden from optical telescopes by dust and gas. Two of its most important scientific instruments were IRAC and MIPS, each contributing uniquely to the mission's success.

## IRAC (Infrared Array Camera)

IRAC was one of three science instruments aboard Spitzer, functioning as a four-channel camera that captured images simultaneously at wavelengths of 3.6, 4.5, 5.8, and 8.0 microns. This capability made IRAC particularly valuable for studying a wide range of astronomical objects, from nearby stars and planetary systems to distant galaxies in the early universe. The instrument's sensitivity to these specific infrared wavelengths allowed astronomers to peer through interstellar dust clouds that would otherwise obscure visible light, revealing star-forming regions and the structure of galaxies in unprecedented detail.

## MIPS (Multiband Imaging Photometer for Spitzer)

MIPS complemented IRAC by observing at longer infrared wavelengths—24, 70, and 160 microns. This instrument was specifically designed to detect cooler cosmic material, such as dust in debris disks around stars, the interstellar medium, and distant, dust-obscured galaxies. MIPS played a crucial role in studying thermal emission from celestial objects, providing insights into star formation processes, planetary system formation, and the life cycles of galaxies.

## Scientific Legacy

Together, IRAC and MIPS enabled Spitzer to make significant contributions to astrophysics. The telescope's instruments helped detect exoplanets, map the structure of the Milky Way, study brown dwarfs, and observe some of the most distant galaxies ever recorded. Spitzer's infrared capabilities were particularly crucial because many cosmic processes—including star formation within dense molecular clouds—emit primarily in infrared wavelengths rather than visible light.

Spitzer operated for over 16 years, far exceeding its planned mission duration, before being decommissioned in January 2020. The data collected by IRAC and MIPS continues to be analyzed by astronomers today, cementing Spitzer's legacy as one of the most productive space telescopes in history and paving the way for subsequent infrared observatories, including the James Webb Space Telescope.

We present a comprehensive infrared study of young stellar objects (YSOs) in the Serpens star-forming region using photometric data obtained with the Infrared Array Camera (IRAC) and the Multiband Imaging Photometer for Spitzer (MIPS) aboard the Spitzer Space Telescope. Covering wavelengths from 3.6 to 70 μm, our observations enable the identification and classification of YSOs based on their spectral energy distributions (SEDs) and infrared color-color diagrams, distinguishing between Class 0/I protostars, Class II (classical T Tauri) objects, and more evolved Class III sources with weak or absent infrared excesses.

We identify several hundred candidate YSOs across the Serpens cloud, revealing a spatial distribution that correlates with regions of high extinction and known dense molecular gas clumps traced by prior submillimeter and near-infrared surveys. The derived disk fractions and infrared excess properties allow us to estimate relative ages and evolutionary states across subclusters within the region, indicating that star formation has proceeded in a spatially and temporally structured manner rather than uniformly across the cloud. A subset of sources exhibit SEDs consistent with transition disks, providing candidates for studying disk dissipation timescales.

By combining IRAC and MIPS photometry, we construct a more complete census of the young stellar population than achievable with near-infrared surveys alone, extending sensitivity to lower-mass and more deeply embedded objects. Comparison with X-ray and millimeter continuum data further refines cluster membership and helps mitigate contamination from extragalactic and evolved stellar populations. Our results contribute to a clearer picture of the star formation history, protostellar content, and clustering properties of the Serpens region, offering an important benchmark for comparative studies of clustered low-mass star formation in nearby molecular clouds.

# Abstract

We present a comprehensive analysis of young stellar objects (YSOs) identified in the Serpens molecular cloud as part of the *Spitzer* Space Telescope "Cores to Disks" (c2d) Legacy survey. Using photometry from IRAC (3.6–8.0 μm) and MIPS (24 and 70 μm) combined with ancillary 2MASS near-infrared data, we develop a multi-wavelength color-magnitude classification scheme to distinguish bona fide YSOs from contaminating extragalactic sources and reddened background stars. Our criteria incorporate spectral energy distribution (SED) slopes, infrared color-color diagrams, and detection thresholds across multiple bands to construct a robust, statistically vetted catalog of candidate young stars, yielding a sample of several hundred sources spanning evolutionary stages from deeply embedded protostars (Class 0/I) to pre-main-sequence stars with optically thin disks (Class II/III).

For each identified YSO, we perform SED fitting using a grid of radiative transfer disk models that account for varying disk geometry, accretion rates, envelope density, and inclination, enabling us to constrain physical parameters such as disk mass, inner hole radius, and evolutionary class. We find that approximately 30% of Class II sources exhibit SEDs consistent with transitional or pre-transitional disks, suggesting ongoing grain growth and planet formation processes.

We further conduct a spatial clustering analysis using minimum spanning tree and nearest-neighbor surface density techniques to characterize the distribution of YSOs relative to the cloud's dense gas structure traced by extinction and submillimeter continuum maps. Two dominant clusters are identified, coincident with the previously known Serpens Main and Serpens South regions, exhibiting central stellar densities of order 10²–10³ pc⁻². We derive a disk fraction gradient as a function of cluster-centric distance and local stellar density, finding evidence that disk evolution proceeds more rapidly in high-density subclusters, potentially due to enhanced dynamical interactions or environmental UV irradiation. These results provide new constraints on the star formation history, clustering dynamics, and circumstellar disk evolution within Serpens, and offer a template methodology for analogous analyses in other c2d clouds.

# Distinguishing Young Stellar Objects from Extragalactic Contaminants Using Combined Spitzer IRAC/MIPS Photometry

## Abstract

Infrared surveys of star-forming regions using the *Spitzer Space Telescope* have proven highly effective for identifying young stellar objects (YSOs) through detection of excess emission from circumstellar disks and envelopes. However, extragalactic contaminants—particularly broad-line active galactic nuclei (AGN) and dusty starburst galaxies—exhibit infrared colors that closely mimic those of Class I and Class II YSOs in traditional IRAC color-color diagrams, leading to significant contamination rates in candidate YSO catalogs. We present a refined classification methodology that combines IRAC (3.6–8.0 μm) photometry with MIPS 24 μm data to better discriminate genuine young stars from extragalactic interlopers in a nearby star-forming region. By incorporating the 24 μm band, we access additional diagnostic power from the spectral energy distribution shape at longer wavelengths, where AGN and YSOs diverge more clearly due to differences in dust temperature distributions and the presence or absence of silicate features. We construct a set of empirical color-magnitude and color-color criteria using [3.6]−[4.5], [5.8]−[8.0], and [8.0]−[24] colors, calibrated against spectroscopically confirmed samples of both YSOs and background galaxies. Application of these criteria to our target field reduces the contamination fraction in the YSO candidate list by removing a substantial number of sources previously misclassified based on IRAC colors alone, while retaining the majority of bona fide young stellar objects, including deeply embedded protostars. We characterize the resulting YSO population's spatial distribution, luminosity function, and disk evolutionary stage, finding good agreement with independent indicators such as X-ray emission and near-infrared spectroscopy. Our results demonstrate that the inclusion of MIPS 24 μm photometry substantially improves the fidelity of YSO catalogs derived from mid-infrared surveys, an important consideration for statistical studies of star formation rates, disk lifetimes, and initial mass functions in Galactic star-forming complexes observed with limited follow-up spectroscopic resources.

# Disk Properties, Luminosity Function, and Spatial Clustering of Young Stellar Objects in the Serpens Molecular Cloud: A Spitzer Space Telescope Study

## Abstract

We present a comprehensive analysis of young stellar objects (YSOs) in the Serpens molecular cloud using multi-wavelength photometry from the Spitzer Space Telescope's IRAC (3.6–8.0 μm) and MIPS (24 and 70 μm) instruments, complemented by ground-based near-infrared and millimeter continuum data. Our survey covers approximately 1.5 square degrees encompassing the main cluster regions (Cluster A and Cluster B) and surrounding filamentary structures, resulting in the identification of several hundred candidate YSOs spanning evolutionary stages from deeply embedded protostars (Class 0/I) to more evolved pre-main-sequence stars with optically thin disks (Class III).

Employing spectral energy distribution (SED) slope classification and infrared color-color diagrams, we classify sources into evolutionary stages and derive disk fractions across the cloud, finding an overall disk fraction of order 60–70%, consistent with the young age (~2–4 Myr) inferred for the region. We characterize the distribution of infrared spectral indices (α_IRAC) and 24 μm excess emission to identify transitional and pre-transitional disk candidates, revealing a population of objects with evidence for inner disk clearing. The disk fraction shows spatial variation, being systematically lower in the dense cluster cores compared to the more dispersed population, potentially reflecting either an age gradient or enhanced disk destruction processes in high-stellar-density environments.

We construct the YSO luminosity function (YLF) by integrating dereddened SEDs from near-infrared through far-infrared wavelengths, obtaining bolometric luminosities for the embedded population. The resulting luminosity function is compared to model predictions from various star formation scenarios, including constant versus time-dependent mass accretion histories, and to luminosity functions derived for other nearby star-forming regions (e.g., Ophiuchus, Perseus, Chamaeleon). We find that the observed YLF is best matched by models incorporating episodic or decreasing accretion rates rather than simple constant-accretion scenarios, consistent with the emerging paradigm of episodic accretion in the early stages of stellar mass assembly.

Spatial clustering analysis, employing nearest-neighbor statistics and the minimum spanning tree (MST) technique, reveals that YSOs in Serpens exhibit significant hierarchical clustering, with the youngest (Class 0/I) sources preferentially concentrated in the highest column density filaments traced by (sub)millimeter continuum and extinction maps. We derive a projected surface density map of YSOs and identify distinct sub-clusters with characteristic sizes of 0.1–0.3 pc, embedded within larger-scale filamentary structure extending over several parsecs. The degree of mass segregation and the correlation between local YSO surface density and evolutionary class support a scenario of clustered star formation proceeding along dense filaments, with subsequent dynamical evolution dispersing the youngest sub-clusters on timescales of a few Myr. These results provide important constraints on the initial conditions and early dynamical evolution of embedded clusters, and offer a template for comparison with numerical simulations of clustered star formation in turbulent, filamentary molecular clouds.

**Key words:** stars: formation — stars: pre-main sequence — infrared: stars — open clusters and associations: individual (Serpens) — protoplanetary disks
